Fig. 5. Specific conductivity for various ionic liquids at 25 ◦C. for the FSI−-based ILs than for the TFSI−-based ones, as expected from less Van der Waals interactions from the smaller FSI−. For a given anion, the viscosity generally increases with the increase of cation size in the order of N1.3(1O2)+ < N2.3(1O2)+ < N4(1O2)+, except for the N22.2(1O2)+. The viscosity is unexpectedly lower for the N1.3(1O2)+ than for the N22.2(1O2)+, although the volume of the former cation is larger. It seems that the effect of better flexibility of the ether-containing side chain plays a predominant role over Van der Waals interactions in this case. A comparison between the viscosities of the multimethoxyethyl ammonium ILs and those of the corresponding isoelectronic tetraalkyl substituted ones further displays the impact of multi-ether functional groups on the fluid of ILs. For example, N1444[TFSI] (787 cP at 20 ◦C [74], 386 at 30 ◦C [72]) versus N1.3(1O2)[TFSI] (96 cP at 25 ◦C), and N3333[TFSI] (430 cP at 25 ◦C [71]) versus N22.2(1O2)[TFSI] (101 cP at 25 ◦C) (both cations are isoelectronic). These results suggest that introducing multiether functions into oniums is an elegant approach to obtain low-viscosity and low-melting ILs.
